common_name: Duchesse de Brabant Rose (Cupped Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Duchesse de Brabant is an 1857 tea rose famously worn as a boutonniere by Theodore Roosevelt and prized in Deep South gardens for its cupped, silky pink blooms and outstanding heat tolerance.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1857, Duchesse de Brabant bears silky, cupped, shell-pink blooms with a light, fruity tea fragrance, held on a bushy, rounded shrub with soft blue-green foliage. President Theodore Roosevelt reportedly wore its blooms as a boutonniere, and the rose has remained a favorite of Southern gardens ever since for its dependable, near-continuous bloom and excellent tolerance of heat and humidity. It shows good resistance to blackspot compared with modern hybrid teas and asks for little beyond routine watering once established. The nodding, cupped flower form and soft coloring make it a favorite for cutting and for cottage-style borders. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; avoid hard pruning, which delays and reduces bloom.

common_name: Champneys' Pink Cluster Rose (Original Noisette Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall at the base of a support for its climbing habit; Champneys' Pink Cluster was bred around 1811 by John Champneys of Charleston, South Carolina, and is the founding rose of the entire Noisette class — the only class of roses developed in North America — making it historically significant as well as well adapted to Gulf South heat and humidity.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a fence, arbor, or trellis, allowing 4-6 feet for its spreading, semi-climbing habit. Bred around 1811 by rice planter John Champneys of Charleston, South Carolina, by crossing the musk rose with an early China rose, Champneys' Pink Cluster became the founding parent of the Noisette class — the only major class of roses developed in North America — after cuttings were shared with a Charleston nurseryman named Philippe Noisette, who sent seedlings on to his brother in Paris. It bears large, loose clusters of small, semi-double, soft pink, fragrant blooms in repeated flushes from spring through fall on long, lax canes best trained on a support. As an early hybrid between a China rose and a musk rose, it carries strong heat tolerance and repeat bloom, traits that were unusual in roses available in Europe at the time and that make it well suited to the modern Gulf South garden. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape and remove spent wood, training new canes onto the support as they grow.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Champneys' Pink Cluster variety notes
American Rose Society — Noisette Rose Class Descriptions
Historic Charleston Foundation — Noisette Rose Origins

common_name: Martha Gonzales Rose (Compact Found Texas China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Martha Gonzales is a compact, red-flowered found rose discovered in a Texas dooryard garden and named for the woman who grew it, prized for its small size and reliable, near-continuous bloom in Gulf Coast heat.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart for a low border or mass planting. Martha Gonzales is a 'found rose' — a once-unnamed variety rediscovered growing in a Texas garden and identified and named for the woman who had grown and passed it down within her family — and it has become a favorite dwarf China-type rose valued for its compact, low-mounding habit rarely exceeding 2 feet, unusual among garden roses. It produces small, semi-double, brick-red blooms with a light fragrance in dense flushes almost continuously from spring through frost, and new foliage emerges with an attractive reddish tint. Like other China-type roses, it is exceptionally tolerant of heat and humidity and shows strong resistance to blackspot, needing no spray program even in the Gulf South. Its diminutive size makes it useful for edging beds, low borders, and containers where larger antique roses would overwhelm the space. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or twiggy growth; otherwise it needs very little maintenance.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Martha Gonzales variety notes

common_name: Carefree Beauty Rose (Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Carefree Beauty was bred by Iowa State University professor Griffith Buck as part of a program developing own-root, winter-hardy, disease-resistant roses that need no spraying or winter protection, and it performs equally well across a wide climate range from the northern Midwest to the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Bred by Dr. Griffith Buck at Iowa State University and introduced in 1977, Carefree Beauty is one of the best-known results of his decades-long program to develop tough, own-root roses that survive harsh Midwestern winters without protection and resist disease without spraying — goals that happen to also produce excellent performance in the hot, humid Gulf South. It bears large, semi-double, clear pink blooms with a light fragrance in generous flushes from late spring through fall, followed by an abundant crop of showy orange-red hips that provide fall and winter interest and feed birds. The vigorous, upright shrub shows strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew and needs minimal care once established. Prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, and leave some hips on the plant through fall for ornamental and wildlife value.
sources: Iowa State University — Griffith Buck Rose Breeding Program
American Rose Society — Buck Rose Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Earth-Kind Rose Trials
